reception.text: By November 1907 the fights over joint statehood and the constitution were over, and the new state greeted the signing as a celebration rather than a contest.
On statehood day a mock wedding on the steps of Guthrie's Carnegie Library joined "Mr. Oklahoma Territory," played by C. G. Jones, to "Miss Indian Territory," played by Anna Trainor Bennett.

National opinion on the new constitution split: reformers and Populists praised its railroad and corporate regulation, while conservatives and much of the business press called it dangerously radical.
The statewide prohibition clause was welcomed by the temperance movement and resented by others as a mandate written into the founding document.

political_impact.text: Charles N. Haskell was inaugurated as the first governor, and the new state proved as Democratic as Republicans in Washington had feared.
Statehood ended Indian Territory as a separate territorial jurisdiction, but the Five Tribes' governments continued under the Five Tribes Act of 1906.
Guthrie became the first state capital.
Oklahoma's first legislature passed a separate-coach law, Senate Bill One, approved December 18, 1907.

In his Seventh Annual Message Roosevelt told Congress that Oklahoma now stood on a full equality with the other states, adding that the federal duty to guard the rights of the Indians within its borders remained unchanged.
political_impact.source: Seventh Annual Message, December 3, 1907 (American Presidency Project)

legacy.text: The 1907 constitution is still in force, with no successor document; at about 84,956 words it was the fourth-longest state constitution as of January 1, 2023, with 200 of 376 submitted amendments adopted.
Constitutional prohibition lasted until voters repealed it in 1959; liquor by the drink stayed illegal until 1984, and then only by county option.
The fight over moving the capital to Oklahoma City produced Coyle v. Smith, the leading statement of the equal-footing doctrine for new states.
The Five Tribes' governments, suppressed but never dissolved after statehood, regained the right to elect their own principal officers in 1970.

In McGirt v. Oklahoma the Supreme Court held that Congress never disestablished the Muscogee (Creek) reservation, so the land remains Indian country for federal criminal law; later rulings have narrowed the decision.

today.name: State of Oklahoma
today.note: Admitted as the forty-sixth state; its 1907 constitution remains in force.

later_actions.text: Voters chose to move the capital from Guthrie to Oklahoma City, 96,448 to 64,522; the state supreme court voided the election that November.
The legislature located the capital at Oklahoma City by statute.
The U.S. Supreme Court upheld the capital move, holding that locating a state's seat of government is a state power beyond the control of Congress.
The Oklahoma Indian Welfare Act opened tribal reorganization to Oklahoma tribes.
State Question 386 repealed constitutional prohibition, 396,845 to 314,380; legal package sales began September 1, 1959.
Congress restored popular election of the Five Tribes' principal officers.
State Question 563 allowed liquor by the drink, by county option.
The Supreme Court held 5–4 that the Muscogee (Creek) reservation was never disestablished and remains Indian country under the Major Crimes Act.
The Supreme Court held that the state and federal governments share jurisdiction over crimes by non-Indians against Indians in Indian country, narrowing McGirt without overruling it.
